note_claims.claim: The patient has had recurrent headaches for six months.
The patient experiences two to three episodes of headaches per month.
Headaches are preceded by visual aura (shimmering zigzag lines to one side) lasting about 20 minutes.
The headache is unilateral, usually left-sided, and throbbing.
The headache is accompanied by nausea and photophobia.
The headache lasts most of the day.
The patient has no focal weakness, numbness, or speech disturbance.
The patient has no thunderclap headache.
The patient has no symptoms of migraine without aura in the family (mother has migraine without aura).
The patient is a non-smoker.
The patient has been taking a combined oral contraceptive (Rigevidon) for four years.
The patient takes paracetamol as needed.
The patient's blood pressure is 118/76.
The patient's fundi are normal.
The patient's neurological examination is normal.
The diagnosis is Migraine with aura.
Combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated (UKMEC 4).
The plan is to stop the combined pill and start desogestrel 75 micrograms once daily continuously.
The patient must use condoms for the first two days after starting desogestrel.
Sumatriptan 50 mg should be taken at headache onset (not during aura).
Sumatriptan can be repeated after two hours, with a maximum dose of 300 mg in 24 hours.
Sumatriptan may be taken with paracetamol.
Acute treatment should be limited to two to three days per week to avoid medication-overuse headache.
The patient is advised to keep a headache diary.
The follow-up appointment is scheduled in six weeks.
The patient should call 999 or attend A&E if they experience a sudden severe headache, one-sided weakness or numbness, speech difficulty, or a headache with fever and neck stiffness.

transcript_facts.fact: The clinician initiates the consultation by asking the patient what brought them in.
The patient reports getting headaches that are getting more frequent.
The clinician asks how long the patient has been getting the headaches.
The patient reports having headaches for about six months.
The patient reports having two or three episodes a month.
The clinician asks the patient to describe one headache from the beginning.
The patient describes the headache starting with vision, specifically zigzag lines, shimmering, off to one side.
The clinician asks how long the zigzags last.
The patient initially states the zigzags last about an hour, but corrects themselves, stating they timed it last time and it was twenty minutes.
The clinician notes the duration of the aura as twenty minutes.
The patient states that after the vision thing, the headache comes on one side (usually the left) and throbs.
The clinician asks if anything else accompanies the headache.
The patient reports feeling sick and being unable to stand bright lights, requiring them to lie down in a dark room.
The clinician asks how long the headache lasts.
The patient reports the headache lasts most of the day and they are wiped out the next day.
The clinician asks about weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking with the headache.
The patient reports no weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking, only the vision thing.
The clinician asks if the patient has ever had a sudden, severe headache, like being hit on the head, the worst ever.
The patient reports never having had a sudden, severe headache.
The clinician asks if the headaches are worse when the patient lies down, coughs, or strains.
The patient reports no worsening with lying down, coughing, or straining.
The clinician asks about fevers or stiff neck.
The patient reports no fevers or stiff neck.
The clinician asks if anyone in the family gets migraines.
The patient states their mother has migraines but she never gets the lights (aura).
The clinician asks what the patient is taking for the headaches.
The patient states they take paracetamol, but it doesn't do much.
The patient states they are on the pill (Rigevidon) for about four years.
The clinician asks if the patient smokes.
The patient reports never smoking.
The clinician asks about allergies.
The patient reports no known drug allergies.
The clinician records the patient's blood pressure as 118 over 76.
The clinician notes the back of the eyes look normal.
The clinician notes the nervous system examination is completely normal.
The clinician provides the impression that the condition is Migraine with aura, stating the zigzags are the aura.
The clinician advises that while migraine itself isn't dangerous, the combined pill increases the risk of stroke, making it unsafe to keep taking.
The patient expresses surprise that they were not aware of the stroke risk.
The clinician prescribes stopping the Rigevidon and switching to a progestogen-only pill called desogestrel, 75 micrograms, one every day without a break, stating it doesn't carry that risk.
The clinician asks the patient if they need extra protection.
The clinician advises the patient to use condoms for the first two days after starting desogestrel.
The patient acknowledges the advice.
The clinician prescribes sumatriptan, 50 milligrams, to be taken as soon as the headache starts, not during the zigzags.
The clinician advises that if the headache comes back, the patient can take another after two hours, but no more than 300 milligrams in 24 hours.
The clinician advises that sumatriptan can be taken with paracetamol.
The clinician advises the patient to try not to use painkillers or sumatriptan on more than two or three days a week, because using them too often can cause more headaches.
The clinician advises the patient to keep a headache diary.
The clinician states they will see the patient in six weeks.

The clinician provides safety-netting advice: call 999 or go to A&E if the patient gets a sudden severe headache, weakness or numbness on one side, difficulty speaking, or a headache with fever and a stiff neck.
The patient acknowledges the safety-netting advice and says thank you.
